story_text.value:
In an RTS game, making decisions quickly matters as much as making good ones. Looking for the balance between cost, speed and intelligence in agents, I started wondering what an agent playing an RTS would look like. So I built a simple RTS, and I keep making it more complex.

- The game keeps running while the agent thinks

- The agent can upload a JavaScript script for each unit type

- 300+ game replays

- Connects through MCP or CLI. Works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor CLI, Antigravity CLI, OpenCode, OpenClaw, DeepSeek Harness and MiniMax Code

- 2 to 6 players, FFA and co-op, open and walled maps

- 4 units, the King and 4 buildings

- Open source, written in TypeScript

story_text.value:
Hey HN, I'm Christian and this is a new OSS project I've been noodling on for the last couple of weeks. Hob is a free, MIT-licensed desktop app for Mac, Windows and Linux that works on your files the way the Claude and ChatGPT desktop apps do, except the model runs on your own computer. It uses open-weight models (currently Gemma 4 and gpt-oss). All your chats and files never leave your system. The only things that go online are web search (can be turned off in settings) and any MCP connectors you add yourself.

Main features:

- Automatically finds the best open-weight model for your hardware on first install (Mac/Linux/Windows)

- Writes sandboxed Python code for ad hoc tools (data processing, document conversion, graphs etc.)

- Built-in web search (powered by SearXNG)

- MCP support

- Image recognition

- CRUD to your local filesystem

- Works fully offline with no internet

Before building this I tried every local AI app I could find, but it seemed each one had different problems. The main thing I noticed is that none of them could do what the ChatGPT and Claude apps do with your files, e.g. read and change files in a folder, look at images, run code in a sandbox, draw a chart. The most advanced thing any of them did was paste a plain text file into a small context window, which basically failed as soon as you had a file larger than a few KB. I couldn't find anything that could easily parse images and bigger PDFs.

The OSS solutions that were more advanced all seemed to default to hosted models (either OSS or closed), which defeats the entire point of the privacy that on-device OSS offers. They also seemed to push towards an account/open-core style business.

I build it using Electron bridged with llama.cpp in its own process. On initial load, the system will try and figure out if you have a compatible graphics card and if not default to CPU-only (I ran into a lot of issues of graphics card beeing seemingly compatible but then crashing on first query, there's a whole saga to this lol). Code execution happens in a sandbox that can only write to the chat's folder and has no network unless asked (sandbox-exec on macOS, Landlock on Linux and a low-integrity process on Windows). Images go to a small Qwen3-VL model. Dictation is a local Whisper model.

The hardest part was definitely to get the smaller models to use tools reliably. Ran into a ton of issues of 4B models happily saying "here's your chart" without ever calling the chart tool or get stuck in an infinite call loop. I spent a fair amount of the work building guards vs tweaking prompts (that didn't really work for small models).

I understand the pushback that local models are weaker than frontier cloud models. This is true, but for most tasks for most normal people, I'd argue you rarely need the newest frontier model. From my own evals, systems with 16+ GB of RAM do really well, and if you have a GPU or more RAM, you get very close to what you'll get out of the box with a frontier hosted model.

Excited to hear what you think and see how it runs on other systems!

title.value: Show HN: Hob - Open-source, on device alternative to Claude Cowork and ChatGPT

story_text.value:
Hello HN, I'm Manish and I built LPMR Delta. My background was originally in healthcare and with luck + grit I ended up on the terminal product side of finance. LPMR Delta is out to solve one main issue, overly complex financial terminals.

It's a browser-based terminal for macroeconomic, fundamental, and regulatory research. Right now, it can: 1. Find and download current + historical filings available on SEC 2. A richer and focused Macroeconomic mode i.e. series are made grouped and pinned according to their importance on a daily basis 3. User friendly comparison and export capabilities

It covers US data only for now. I'd rather go deep on one market than spread thin. It started with XBRL filings for equity fundamentals, and I added macro once I hit XBRL's limits.

I made it using FastAPI and Vue.js, kept it simple since this is the first time I've ever coded.

It's freemium: most core functionality is in the free tier with usage limits. You need a free account to get started (no card required).

To be clear, it's not a Bloomberg, LSEG, or FactSet replacement. It's for people who want to do proper research in one place without being buried in excess information.

I would genuinely appreciate any feedback and would love to answer any questions you would have. Thank you again for your time :)

title.value: Show HN: LPMR Delta, a lightweight financial research terminal

story_text.value:
Hi HN!

I made git-dupe to solve the problem where I have notes, skills, and agent instructions that are part of my personal workflow, so I do not want them committed to the public repo, but at the same time, I want them to be in the project at the correct locations (e.g., AGENTS.md file locations matter), and these files cannot be simply gitignored because I want versioning for them.

The solution that I've come upon is versioning those agent files in another repo, say <private-repo> (this repo is private to me and holds the history for my agent files). The project itself is open to the public in another <public-repo>. I overlap the two repos to solve the problem (i.e., they share the same worktree).

  $ git status --short              # the public repo
  ?? AGENTS.md
  ?? notes/

  $ git dupe init                   # the private repo
  Initialized empty Git repository in /home/brian/code/project/.git/dupe/

  $ git dupe add notes/ AGENTS.md   # the private repo
  hint: notes is now hidden from the project's Git; run from the root, 'git dupe unhide -- notes' stops hiding it

  $ git dupe commit -m "Notes and agent instructions"        # the private repo
  [main (root-commit) 3eb3af9] Notes and agent instructions
   3 files changed, 3 insertions(+)
   create mode 100644 .gitdupe
   create mode 100644 AGENTS.md
   create mode 100644 notes/todo.md

  $ git status --short              # the public repo: nothing

  $ git dupe log --oneline          # the private repo: your files
  3eb3af9 Notes and agent instructions
In short, git-dupe allows two Git repos to share the same worktree, while using native Git for most operations. Most git-dupe commands behave just like normal Git commands, operating on the private repo instead.

git-dupe currently supports Linux and macOS, and is under the MIT License; the git-dupe repo contains much more extensive technical documentation documentation for those who are interested. If you have any feedback/questions about git-dupe, feel free to message. I hope it helps!

Fun fact: the git-dupe project itself is using git-dupe for versioning.

title.value: Show HN: git-dupe – Version private files alongside a public Git repo

story_text.value:
I built sturnus because I wanted the latency-based load balancing of an AI gateway but without a big framework selling an enterprise plan.

It’s a single static binary that does one thing, aiming to avoid the large surface area and security issues that have plagued some LLM gateways.

Traffic is distributed by LLM provider latency and availability. The share going to other providers acts as a probe, so that a recovered provider wins back traffic automatically.

I’ve been running this in prod for a while, feedback, opinions and contributions welcome!

story_text.value:
Hi HackerNews,

My name is Matija, and I'm building ranwhat.com. It's used for checking if any of your secrets have leaked, and where they leaked. It's mostly aimed at solo devs such as myself, but also at anyone using a coding agent. The tool also checks if your coding agent ran any sketchy commands. This is mostly a "better safe than sorry" feature, so you can tell your Claude or Codex not to run them.

The project is open source (MIT) and everything runs locally on your machine.

How to install it: pip install ranwhat / uv tool install ranwhat, or brew install MatijaMiki/ranwhat/ranwhat

There is a free and a paid plan. Everything local is free; the paid plan is 12€ a month and adds server-side features, which you can read more about here: https://ranwhat.com/pricing

All I'm asking for here is feedback, and if you have anything you would want added to the project.

Looking forward to answering any questions you have.

Best, Matija

story_text.value:
I kept finding myself wanting a way to get talked through the code that a model had created, which led to me making Sóþspell (old English, "Truth Story").

You give it a git repo locally or via URL, and it creates a tour of the repo in a web page, with the aim of it explaining the whole thing. There's also model harness plugins for Claude, Codex, and OpenCode.

You give it an API key for whatever model you prefer to create the tour (saved locally or via github), and you can also give it a voice using an ElevenLabs API key.

I just pushed a canvas view, which I'm hoping I can make the code navigation a bit more helpful.

There's a demo codebase, and you can export tours as JSON. The demo doesn't need any keys to work, it falls back to browser speech if you want to hear that.

This is my first real, "big" open source project that I've released, prior to this I'd just contributed stuff. I hope it can be useful to someone! I would love to hear some constructive criticism too, and any suggestions on features you'd like to see.

It's MIT licensed, and I'll try to stick around in the comments to answer questions if people want.

story_text.value:
Hi HN. A while ago I started building a generic people matching app based on LLM-as-a-judge. I needed a way to bypass the O(n^2) "everyone rates everyone else" trap, but generic RAG was much worse than expected.

DNA is a search-like API at the core of that product. It stores one embedding per item (like a vector DB) and gives the best match(es). You evaluate them in some way (LLM / Decision Model / users), and send the score back. This makes it improve in real time, so next time it gives you better results. In my tests, it needed 7x fewer LLM judgments than scoring down the embedding list. Paper in progress.

What I don’t know yet is what demo would make you want to try building with it. What would you want to see it do?
